passage: Four students in one hostel each turned an idea into a business in a different way. Hrithik jotted down everything that annoyed him about hostel life: slow laundry, mess quarrels, noisy corridors. He circled the one his neighbours brought up most often. Vishal, before he built a single thing, sat down with twenty residents and asked how they got their clothes washed and what they paid. To his surprise, price mattered to them far more than an app would. Vandana adored her idea. Friends cheered, and she brushed aside the polite doubts. She poured her savings into a logo plus a website before any stranger had said they wanted the product. Aarav and his partner noticed that customers came mainly at exam time to print their notes. They shrank the idea to a service for printing notes, and orders began to climb.

qa.q: How many residents did Vishal talk to?
qa.a: Vishal talked to twenty residents.

qa.q: How does Vandana's way of testing her idea differ from Vishal's, and what did each learn?
qa.a: Vandana heard only cheering from friends and spent savings on a logo and website before checking demand. Vishal spoke to twenty residents first and learned that price mattered more than an app.

qa.q: What might Vandana be feeling as she brushes aside the polite doubts?
qa.a: She is probably excited and attached to her idea, and worried that doubts might spoil it.

qa.q: What could Vandana do now?
qa.a: She could show the product to strangers who might use it and listen for honest doubts, then decide what to change. Asking a few people to be frank would help. 🙂

grounding: Students turn a hostel idea into a startup by listing daily problems, interviewing users, falling for the idea, and pivoting to what customers use.

passage: Four founders were planning to raise money, each in a different way. Madhav decided he needed eighteen months of runway. He calculated the sum, then counted back to how many investor meetings he would need, when the pitch had to be ready and what numbers he must show by then. Aadhya wrote down sixty angels and early-stage funds that had funded health-tech firms in India, ranked them by fit and by who could introduce her, and logged every contact on a sheet the team could all open. Yamini's team mailed an identical deck to 200 investors. Most said no within a day because the startup did not match what they looked for, and hours of the team's time went on mass emails. Tanvi's team heard fifteen rejections that all raised the same worry. She stopped pitching, signed three pilot customers to close the gap in traction, and went back with better evidence.

qa.q: How many investors did Yamini's team email?
qa.a: Yamini's team emailed two hundred investors.

qa.q: How does Yamini's team's outreach differ from Aadhya's, and what result did each get?
qa.a: Yamini's team sent one deck to two hundred investors without research and mostly got fast rejections. Aadhya listed sixty investors who had backed similar startups, ranked by fit and introductions, and tracked each.

qa.q: What might Tanvi be feeling after fifteen rejections?
qa.a: She is probably discouraged and worried, but she takes the pattern seriously and turns it into something to fix.

qa.q: What could Yamini's team do differently before sending more emails?
qa.a: They could research which investors back startups like theirs and pick a short list to approach with a fitting pitch. Learning from the quick rejections would help too. 🙂

grounding: Four founders plan a funding round by working backward from a target, listing investors, mass pitching without research, and fixing the story after repeated rejections.

passage: Four boys in Class 9 each liked a classmate and went about it differently. Jatin pictured himself inviting Riya along to a study session with several classmates, chose words that would be easy to turn down, and prepared a calm reply for a yes or a no. Vijay spent a few weeks talking with Sana about the robotics club and their project, noticing whether she seemed at ease, before he suggested a casual meet-up with others. Harsha had seen a film and planned to ask Meher while the entire class watched, holding flowers. But with everyone watching, it would be hard for her to answer comfortably, and she might feel embarrassed whatever she said. Kabir asked Pooja to a school event, and she politely said no. He thanked her, gave her space, spent his evenings with friends and on the football ground, and reminded himself that disappointment fades. He kept chatting normally in class, and it stayed comfortable.

qa.q: Whom did Jatin plan to ask to the study session?
qa.a: Jatin planned to ask Riya to join a group study session.

qa.q: How does Harsha's plan differ from Vijay's approach, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Harsha planned a public gesture in front of the whole class, which pressures the other person. Vijay built a friendly connection over weeks and suggested a casual group meet-up, so it stays comfortable for her.

qa.q: What might Kabir be feeling after Pooja says no?
qa.a: He is probably disappointed and a little embarrassed, but he stays polite and gives her space.

qa.q: What could Harsha do instead of a public gesture?
qa.a: He could ask Meher privately and calmly, with words that are easy to decline, and accept the answer kindly. Getting to know her first would help too.

grounding: Four boys approach a crush by rehearsing a low-pressure invitation, building friendship first, planning a grand public gesture, and recovering after a polite no.

passage: A college senior told Vaibhav that a scheme paid ten percent every month. Vaibhav asked himself what would need to hold for such a thing to be genuine, and saw that no lawful arrangement can promise such a return. Imagining the trap first showed him the warning signs, so he walked away. Jatin checked before paying anything. He looked up if the platform and its adviser had registered with the market regulator, and read reviews and complaints. Brief homework took the place of trusting a smooth pitch. Rehana saw friends posting screenshots of gains. Within an hour she joined a tip group on a chat app and transferred her savings, and the fear of missing out shut down any checking. The money could not be recovered. Kiran's app asked for one more fee before releasing his money. He saw the pattern, stopped paying, kept copies of the messages and screen captures, and lodged complaints with his bank and on the cybercrime portal.

qa.q: What return did the college senior promise Vaibhav each month?
qa.a: The senior promised ten percent every month.

qa.q: How does Rehana's decision differ from Jatin's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Rehana rushed in within an hour after seeing friends' screenshots and could not recover her money. Jatin checked the platform and adviser's registration and read complaints before paying.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she joined the tip group?
qa.a: She felt pressure and fear of missing out, which pushed her to act before checking.

qa.q: What could Rehana do now?
qa.a: She could stop sending money, keep every chat and screenshot, tell a trusted adult and report to her bank and the cybercrime portal. Reporting early can limit further harm. 🤍

grounding: Four young people meet an investment scam by asking how it could be a trap, checking registration, rushing from fear of missing out, and reporting when withdrawals are blocked.

passage: Four children were getting ready for the school programme, each in a different way. Deepika split her part in the play into four scenes and learned one each day, so the long script felt less scary and she could see her progress. Madhav practised his poem after dinner with his whole family watching. They urged him to go slower and raise his eyes, and by the day itself he had improved. Leela kept singing the opening verse of her song again and again because she loved it. On stage she felt sure of herself at first, then forgot the second verse, which she had hardly practised. Arnav recorded his speech using his mother's mobile and heard that he spoke too fast and mumbled the last lines. He tried stopping briefly after every sentence and recorded it again to compare the two.

qa.q: Where did Madhav practise his poem?
qa.a: He practised in front of his family after dinner.

qa.q: How does Leela's way of practising differ from Deepika's, and what happened on stage?
qa.a: Leela repeated only the verse she loved and forgot the second verse on stage. Deepika learned one scene each day and could check her progress.

qa.q: What might Leela be feeling when she forgets the second verse?
qa.a: She is probably nervous and embarrassed, since her confidence at the start gave way to a blank.

qa.q: What could Leela do to prepare next time?
qa.a: She could practise the parts she finds hard first, or the whole song from start to finish, and sing it for someone at home. 🙂

grounding: Children prepare for a school performance by splitting the piece, rehearsing before family, repeating only what they know, and recording themselves.

passage: Madhuri, who was learning the harmonium, played for fifteen minutes each evening straight after her snack. Because the time was fixed, she never had to choose one each day. Lalit could not get past a tricky tabla piece. He played just the opening pair of beats at a crawl, then added the following ones, reasoning that a difficult tune is only lots of easy bits joined up. Joseph kept playing the simple beginning of his song over and over because it sounded nice. The tough middle never got better, and every lesson felt the same as the last. Sneha's guitar teacher pointed out that her fingers sat in the wrong place on one chord, and it kept sounding muffled. She slowed down, watched her fingers in a mirror, and moved her fingers until the chord rang out clearly.

qa.q: When did Madhuri practise the harmonium each day?
qa.a: She practised for fifteen minutes each evening straight after her snack.

qa.q: How does Joseph's practice differ from Lalit's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Joseph kept playing the easy opening, so the hard middle never improved. Lalit built the piece beat by beat, so the hard part became many small easy ones.

qa.q: What might Joseph be feeling as each lesson feels the same?
qa.a: He is probably bored or discouraged, because he keeps playing the same easy bit and sees no progress.

qa.q: What could Joseph try at his next practice?
qa.a: He could start with the hard middle and play it slowly, a few beats at a time, and ask his teacher to check what needs work. 🙂

grounding: Children learn an instrument with a fixed daily slot, breaking a piece into parts, repeating only the easy opening, and using a teacher's feedback.
